case_name: Pankaj Chhabildas Sheth v. Abhyudaya Co-Operative Bank Ltd.
citation: (2026) ibclaw.in 1031 NCLAT; also cited as 2026 TAXSCAN (NCLAT) 226
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (Principal Bench, New Delhi)
holding_summary: Pankaj Chhabildas Sheth, a director and personal guarantor of M/s Veer Wires Private Limited, had guaranteed credit facilities extended by Abhyudaya Co-Operative Bank Ltd.; an arbitral award dated 23 June 2023 held the corporate debtor and its guarantors jointly and severally liable for Rs. 4.20 crore plus 14.5% interest. Sheth's Section 94 IBC application seeking his own insolvency resolution was ultimately dismissed by NCLT as an attempt to obtain an interim moratorium and obstruct the bank's lawful recovery and SARFAESI enforcement rather than a genuine bid at resolution and repayment planning. NCLAT dismissed Sheth's appeal, holding Section 94 applications must be pursued in good faith for actual insolvency resolution, not as a shield against creditor enforcement.
why_it_matters: Signals that NCLAT will scrutinise a personal guarantor's Section 94 application for bona fides and will not permit the interim moratorium it triggers to be used tactically to stall SARFAESI or other recovery proceedings — relevant to both guarantors and secured creditors litigating parallel recovery and personal-insolvency matters.

case_name: Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd. v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission & Anr.
citation: APTEL, order dated on or about 28-29 September 2026, setting aside MERC order dated 30 May 2019
holding_summary: Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd. (SIIPL) operates wind power plants totalling 57.2 MW across Dhule, Sangli and Satara districts in Maharashtra, consuming the power captively and supplying surplus to third-party consumers through Open Access. During April 2016-March 2018, Open Access restrictions prevented delivery of generated power to SIIPL's intended consumers, causing over 3.67 crore units of surplus wind energy to be injected into the state grid instead; MERC rejected SIIPL's claim for compensation by an order dated 30 May 2019. APTEL set aside MERC's rejection and directed MERC to determine, together with applicable carrying costs, the amount payable to SIIPL by Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. for the surplus energy injected during the restricted period.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a captive generator is entitled to compensation for surplus energy injected into the grid when regulatory Open Access restrictions prevent its delivery to the generator's own consumers, reinforcing that a distribution licensee cannot retain the benefit of such injected power without payment.

case_name: State of Odisha and Others v. Dhanurdhar Champatiray
citation: Orissa High Court, decided 21 September 2026 (Routray, J.)
holding_summary: Nine writ petitions challenged orders of District Judges, sitting as appellate authorities under Section 37(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The respondents raised a common preliminary objection that, since the Arbitration Act bars a second appeal against such orders (an appeal lying only to the Supreme Court), the writ petitions were an impermissible substitute for a second appeal. Justice B.P. Routray rejected the objection, holding that the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 is not an appellate remedy and cannot be curtailed by a statutory bar on second appeals, though he confirmed that such supervisory jurisdiction over a Section 37 order remains confined to cases of egregious illegality, perversity or a patent lack of jurisdiction.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a party left without a further statutory appeal after a Section 37 order is not without recourse and can still invoke the High Court's limited supervisory writ jurisdiction, though only in cases of serious jurisdictional or legal error rather than as a routine further round of merits review.

case_name: Sandeep Kumar Bhagat v. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
citation: NCLT Guwahati Bench, decided 10 September 2026
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Guwahati Bench
holding_summary: Three group companies — Shree Sai Prakash Alloys Pvt. Ltd., Shree Sai Rolling Mills (India) Ltd. and Shree Sai Smelters (India) Ltd. — had been funded by Punjab National Bank, were classified as NPAs, went through CIRP, and were ordered into liquidation on 25 January 2024. Sandeep Kumar Bhagat, through his legal heirs, proposed a Rs. 22.50 crore one-time settlement to PNB and alleged the bank failed to consider the proposal despite being notified. The NCLT Guwahati Bench refused to direct PNB to accept the OTS proposal, holding that accepting a one-time settlement is a matter of commercial discretion for the lender and that the Tribunal has no power to compel a financial creditor to accept a settlement that was never crystallised into a binding agreement, particularly once liquidation has already commenced.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a borrower, or heirs acting for one, cannot use the NCLT to force a bank's hand on a proposed one-time settlement once liquidation has begun — accepting or rejecting an OTS remains a commercial call for the lender, not a direction the tribunal will issue.

case_name: In re: Composite Scheme of Arrangement among Parle Products Pvt. Ltd., Parle Biscuits Pvt. Ltd. and Parle Brands Pvt. Ltd.
citation: NCLT, Mumbai Bench, second-motion order dated 23 September 2026 (first-motion order dated 19 June 2026)
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench
holding_summary: NCLT Mumbai's second-motion order sanctioned a composite scheme of arrangement among Parle Products Pvt. Ltd., Parle Biscuits Pvt. Ltd. and newly-incorporated Parle Brands Pvt. Ltd., under which Parle Products' processed-food and captive wind-power undertakings are demerged into Parle Brands, Parle Products is then amalgamated into Parle Biscuits (with Parle Products shareholders receiving 15 equity shares of Parle Brands, plus equity shares and OCRPS of Parle Biscuits, for every 100 shares held), and Parle Biscuits' own processed-food and ancillary business is further demerged into Parle Brands. The bench (Technical Member Prabhat Kumar and Judicial Member Sushil Mahadeorao Kochey) found the scheme fair, reasonable and not contrary to law or public policy, ordered Parle Products dissolved without winding up, and directed the companies to file certified copies of the order and scheme with the Registrar of Companies within 30 days.
why_it_matters: Illustrates the multi-step demerger-cum-amalgamation structure large private groups are using to separate processed-food and ancillary operations from real-estate and brand-holding businesses, including the mixed equity-and-OCRPS consideration mechanics an NCLT will accept as fair in a closely-held group restructuring.

case_name: Breach Candy Swimming Bath Trust & Ors. v. Rajesh Somnath Nerkar
citation: Writ Petition No. 9972 of 2026, decided 1 September 2026
holding_summary: Justice Sandeep V. Marne dismissed a writ petition filed under Article 227 by the Breach Candy Swimming Bath Trust against a Controlling Authority order directing it to pay Rs. 11,67,785 in gratuity (with 10% interest) to its former manager of 23 years, Rajesh Somnath Nerkar, whose services were terminated in 2023 over an alleged Rs. 5 crore loss from shredded membership records. The Court held that the Trust could not bypass the statutory appeal remedy under Section 7(7) of the Payment of Gratuity Act by directly invoking Article 227 after the limitation period for that appeal had lapsed, and that the Trust's absence from the gratuity proceedings (which went ex parte) was of its own making. It imposed Rs. 1 lakh in costs on the Trust.
why_it_matters: A reminder that an employer disputing a gratuity order must pursue the statutory appeal within time rather than seeking a writ as an afterthought, and that unproven loss allegations will not excuse non-payment.

case_name: Amazon Seller Services Private Limited v. Goodluck Buildtech Pvt. Ltd.
citation: O.M.P.(I) (COMM.) 443/2026, Delhi High Court, order dated 28 September 2026
holding_summary: Amazon sought Section 9 interim relief to access and remove its assets from a leased logistics facility (Horizon Urban Logistics Park, Alipur) after terminating its lease with Goodluck Buildtech, which contested the termination citing force majeure. Justice Om Prakash Shukla appointed former Supreme Court judge Justice S. Ravindra Bhat as sole arbitrator for the dispute, which involves an indemnity claim of roughly Rs. 182.50 crore and fixtures/fit-outs worth about Rs. 120 crore, and appointed a Local Commissioner to inspect and inventory Amazon's assets at the premises pending arbitration.
why_it_matters: A practical illustration of how courts use a Local Commissioner under Section 9 to preserve and inventory disputed assets at a leased commercial property while a high-value arbitration is set up, rather than leaving a party to self-help remedies.

case_name: Incyte Holdings Corporation & Anr. v. Melody Healthcare Pvt. Ltd.
citation: CS(COMM) 1054/2026, Delhi High Court, order dated 24 September 2026
holding_summary: Justice Vikas Mahajan granted Incyte an ex parte ad interim injunction restraining Melody Healthcare from making, selling or exporting products containing ruxolitinib, finding a prima facie case of infringement of Indian Patent No. 269841 (valid until 12 December 2026). The Court relied on Melody's listing of 'Ruxolitinib Phosphate' in its API product list and as a supplier on Pharmacompass, and a September 2026 investigation report showing Melody held a Maharashtra FDA manufacturing licence for the API and had developed a generic in-house, treating this as an offer for sale under Section 48 of the Patents Act even absent an actual launch.
why_it_matters: The second ex parte injunction this year over the same ruxolitinib patent (after a similar order against Aurore Life Sciences in July 2026) confirms Delhi High Court's willingness to treat API listings and manufacturing-licence preparations, not just an actual product launch, as sufficient 'offer for sale' infringement to justify an interim injunction ahead of a patent's expiry.

case_name: Sami-Sabinsa Group Ltd. & Ors. and Kerry Inc. v. Union of India, FSSAI & Ministry of AYUSH
citation: Karnataka High Court, interim order (vacation bench)
holding_summary: Health-supplement manufacturers, including Kerry Inc. and a group led by Sami-Sabinsa, challenged an FSSAI advisory (16 April 2026) and a Ministry of AYUSH directive (15 April 2026) restricting use of ashwagandha leaves in supplements, arguing that a restriction of this kind required a formal amendment to the Food Safety and Standards Regulations, 2016 rather than an advisory, and that the underlying studies did not establish a safety risk. Justice S.R. Krishna Kumar, sitting as vacation bench, granted an interim stay of both the advisory and the directive, preserving the status quo for manufacturers and exporters pending further hearing.
why_it_matters: A reminder that FSSAI cannot use an informal advisory to restrict an ingredient already permitted under the 2016 Regulations — any such restriction needs a formal regulatory amendment, giving affected manufacturers a ready administrative-law challenge to similar advisories.

case_name: Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Ltd. (TANGEDCO/TNPDCL) v. Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission & Techno Electric & Engineering Co. Ltd.
citation: Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, order dated 10 August 2026
holding_summary: In a dispute over the Average Power Purchase Cost cap applicable to Techno Electric's 111.90 MW wind capacity in Tamil Nadu, APTEL (Officiating Chairperson Seema Gupta and Judicial Member Virender Bhat) condoned TNPDCL's 632-day delay in filing its appeal against a TNERC order that had ruled for the generator, while directing TNPDCL to pay Rs. 1 lakh in costs to Techno Electric. TNERC had held on 9 July 2024, and clarified on 28 January 2025, that the tariff cap under TNPDCL's April 2022 circular should use the SECI bid tariff of the corresponding year rather than the year of commissioning.
why_it_matters: Shows APTEL remains willing to condone even very long delays by a discom in appealing an adverse tariff order, provided costs are imposed — generators should not assume a long-delayed discom appeal is time-barred as a matter of course.

case_name: Eastern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited v. Daulat
citation: NCLAT, Principal Bench, order dated 25 September 2026
holding_summary: NCLAT (Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma, Judicial Member, with Technical Members Arun Baroka and Indevar Pandey) set aside an NCLT order refusing to recall the 2023 dismissal-for-non-prosecution of a Rs. 20.72 crore electricity-dues claim by a statutory power distribution company, holding that the company's engaged counsel could not simply hand the brief to a junior and stop appearing, and that such deliberate non-appearance by counsel — as distinct from ordinary negligence — should not be visited on the litigant. Invoking Section 238A of the IBC read with Section 5 of the Limitation Act, the Tribunal recalled the dismissal and restored the claim to NCLT for a merits decision.
why_it_matters: Gives claimants in CIRP/liquidation proceedings a basis to seek recall of a dismissal caused by their own counsel's deliberate default, rather than losing a substantial claim purely to a lawyer's conduct.

case_name: Moser Baer Solar Ltd. Liquidator v. JFC Finance (India) Ltd. & Ors.
citation: Supreme Court, order dated 1 October 2026
holding_summary: In the Moser Baer Solar liquidation asset auction, NCLAT had directed the liquidator to immediately refund JFC Finance's Rs. 54 crore deposit after a higher bid (totalling Rs. 168 crore) displaced JFC in a fresh auction, holding the return condition in the auction documents had been triggered. On the liquidator/Committee of Creditors' appeal, a Bench of Justices S.V.N. Bhatti and N.V. Anjaria issued notice and directed the parties to maintain status quo on the deposit pending further hearing, with the dispute centring on whether the liquidator may withhold the deposit until the successful bidder pays the full sale consideration.
why_it_matters: An auction participant's deposit in an IBC liquidation sale is not automatically releasable the moment a higher bid displaces them — the liquidator can press to retain it as security until the new bidder actually completes payment, a point now before the Supreme Court.

case_name: Round Pay Voice Tech v. State of U.P. & Ors.
citation: Allahabad High Court
holding_summary: A show cause notice dated 7 May 2022 under Section 74 of the GST Act had proposed recovery of Rs. 57.60 crore (tax, interest and penalty) for July 2017-March 2018, but the final order dated 5 February 2025 raised the demand to Rs. 59.20 crore, the excess being an additional Rs. 1.60 crore penalty. A Bench of Justices Abdhesh Kumar Chaudhary and Shekhar B. Saraf held the order was ex facie contrary to Section 75(7) of the GST Act, which bars a demand exceeding the amount specified in the show cause notice, rejected the State's argument that statutory interest/penalty could be added regardless of the notice, quashed the order, and remanded the matter for a fresh order after giving the petitioner a hearing on the show cause notice as issued.
why_it_matters: A clean, reusable precedent for any taxpayer facing a final GST order that exceeds the show cause notice amount, however the department tries to justify the excess as 'statutory' interest or penalty — Section 75(7) is applied as an absolute ceiling, not a guideline.

case_name: Darzi (India) LLP & Anr. v. Mr. Akhil Jain
citation: CS(COMM) 1027/2026, Delhi High Court
holding_summary: Justice A.J. Bhambhani granted an ex parte ad interim injunction restraining a clothing business run by the defendant from using the 'Men's Darzi' mark, finding the plaintiff (owner of the 'Darzi' mark) had made out a prima facie case of infringement/passing off and that the balance of convenience favoured an immediate injunction pending further hearing.
why_it_matters: Another example of Delhi High Court's readiness to grant an ex parte injunction against a confusingly similar composite mark at the first hearing itself, without waiting for the defendant's response, where the core element of an established mark is simply prefixed or suffixed with a generic word.

case_name: Sanjay Kumar Singh v. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
citation: Patna High Court, order dated 1 October 2026
holding_summary: A rice mill proprietor who had reached a one-time settlement with PNB's Kutumba branch on 29 December 2021 fixing his liability at Rs. 25.70 lakh, and who claimed to have paid Rs. 20 lakh and offered the balance, sought a writ directing the bank to accept the remaining amount and honour the settlement after the bank refused. Justice G. Anupama Chakravarthy disposed of the writ petition, holding that writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked for recovery-related disputes, including enforcement of a one-time settlement, where an effective alternative remedy exists under the SARFAESI Act, and gave the petitioner liberty to approach the appropriate forum, directing that authority to consider the question of limitation.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a borrower cannot bypass the SARFAESI/DRT route merely by framing a bank's refusal to honour an OTS as a breach to be enforced by writ — the dispute, including whether the OTS is binding, must go through the statutory recovery forum.

case_name: RBI enforcement action against Bank of Baroda
citation: Reserve Bank of India, order dated 30 June 2026, under Section 47A(1)(c) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
holding_summary: The RBI imposed a monetary penalty of Rs. 63.60 lakh on Bank of Baroda for non-compliance with its Fair Practices Code for Lenders and KYC directions, following a statutory inspection of the bank's compliance with regulatory directions.
why_it_matters: Part of a steady drumbeat of RBI enforcement penalties through 2026 on major banks for Fair Practices Code and KYC lapses, underscoring that even large scheduled banks remain exposed to recurring compliance penalties on routine lending-conduct and customer-identification requirements.

case_name: Eastern Division (Projects) Engineers Cooperative Society Ltd. v. State Bank of India & Ors.
citation: Calcutta High Court, order dated on or about 6 October 2026
holding_summary: The ESI Recovery Officer had issued garnishee orders (dated 21 and 26 February 2025) against SBI's Murgasol branch account of the petitioner cooperative society and, when the bank could not remit funds, branded the bank a 'deemed defaulter.' Justice Shampa Dutt (Paul) quashed the garnishee orders, holding SBI could not have remitted ESI dues from what was, on the record, an inoperative account, and that branding the bank a deemed defaulter in these circumstances was without application of mind and violated natural justice. An earlier Division Bench order had allowed the society to operate the account in the ordinary course while keeping Rs. 5 lakh frozen.
why_it_matters: A bank cannot be penalised as a 'defaulter' for failing to comply with a garnishee order against an account that is factually inoperative or frozen — recovery officers must verify the account's actual operability before escalating non-compliance against the bank itself.

case_name: Crystal Crop Protection Limited / FMC India Private Limited (combination notice)
citation: Competition Commission of India, approval reported 1-3 October 2026
holding_summary: The CCI approved Crystal Crop Protection Limited's acquisition of 100% shareholding of FMC India Private Limited, clearing the Indian antitrust leg of FMC Corporation's USD 252 million divestment of its India commercial crop-protection business (agreed 7 May 2026) to Crystal Crop, which also takes a licence to sell FMC-branded crop-protection products in India. The transaction remains subject to other customary closing conditions, with FMC expecting closing by end of 2026.
why_it_matters: One of the larger agrochemical sector consolidations of 2026, relevant to agri-input dealers, distributors and farmers who rely on FMC-branded crop-protection products, since post-closing the Indian distribution/registration holder for those brands changes to Crystal Crop.

case_name: Aayush Bansal & Ors. v. Tata SIA Airlines Ltd.
citation: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Chandigarh, order dated on or about 30 April 2026
court: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Chandigarh
holding_summary: Passengers stranded at Denpasar Airport on their return journey after the airline moved their flight earlier without prior notice, forcing them to buy replacement tickets (about Rs. 51,000) and causing them to miss a connecting Delhi flight, complained of deficiency in service. The Commission enhanced the compensation awarded to Rs. 50,000, affirmed a refund with interest, and awarded litigation costs, holding that timely notice of schedule changes is a basic airline obligation.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that an airline's failure to proactively notify passengers of a preponed (not just delayed) flight is itself an independent deficiency in service attracting enhanced compensation, distinct from ordinary delay-compensation claims.

case_name: Himachal Pradesh Power Transmission Corporation Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & POWERGRID
citation: Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, order dated on or about 24 July 2026
holding_summary: In a dispute traced to a CERC order of 21 November 2019 approving POWERGRID's Commercial Operation Date for transformer-augmentation assets at the Hamirpur substation, APTEL upheld CERC's order that HPPTCL is liable to bear transmission charges on two 220 kV bays from 31 March 2019 until commissioning of its own associated downstream transmission line, and separately held that the 2016 amendment to the Indian Electricity Grid Code requiring an Implementation Agreement could not be applied retrospectively to the pre-existing arrangement.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a state transmission utility cannot avoid liability for charges on a connected central transmission asset simply because its own downstream works are delayed, and that later IEGC amendments imposing new procedural requirements (like an Implementation Agreement) do not reach back to arrangements predating the amendment.

case_name: S.V. Ramasamy v. [Liquidator], Swastik Spinners
citation: NCLAT, Chennai Bench, order reported on or about 1 October 2026
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), Chennai
holding_summary: Ramasamy, a personal guarantor and promoter of Swastik Spinners, had personally settled the company's dues to its financial creditor Tamil Nadu Mercantile Bank for Rs. 9.50 crore under a one-time settlement, after which the bank accepted payment and issued an account closure certificate; he then sought financial creditor status (and effectively, withdrawal of liquidation) on that basis. NCLAT held he could not claim financial creditor status because there was no assignment of TMB's debt in his favour and he had never sought substitution of TMB in the liquidation proceedings — at most, he could be seen as a promoter who had bought the company's assets in a private sale, not as its financial creditor. An earlier NCLT order (May 2023) rejecting withdrawal of liquidation on the same basis had already attained finality.
why_it_matters: A personal guarantor or promoter who pays off a company's debt out of pocket does not step into the shoes of the original financial creditor merely by virtue of payment — without a formal assignment or court-ordered substitution, the payment buys no standing in the insolvency process.

case_name: [Buyer] v. [Seller] (Greater Kailash property specific performance suits)
citation: CS(OS) 394/2025 and CS(OS) 626/2025, Delhi High Court, order dated 6 July 2026
holding_summary: In connected suits for specific performance of an agreement to sell a Greater Kailash property for Rs. 24.50 crore, where the buyer claimed to have already paid most of the price, Justice Amit Bansal granted an interim injunction and status quo over the property after finding the seller had subsequently sold it to a third party, and directed the seller to deposit Rs. 20.5 crore in court pending final adjudication, expressly noting the observations were only prima facie.
why_it_matters: Shows a practical remedy available to a specific-performance plaintiff facing a seller who has sold the same property to someone else mid-suit: an interim order compelling the seller to secure the disputed consideration in court, rather than leaving the buyer to an eventual, harder-to-enforce damages claim.
